details.tagline: Building for One Use Case, Testing Immediately
details.whyNow: Abstract theory without empirical validation is just speculation. But we can't test everything at once - we need to build deep capability in one domain first. By focusing on a single coordination problem (likely democratic decision-making under adversarial pressure), we can build minimal viable simulation infrastructure while immediately providing practical value to researchers and organizations who have policy proposals they want to test. This creates a feedback loop: testing real proposals improves our infrastructure, which enables better testing.
details.whatWereDoing: We're building multi-agent simulation infrastructure for one specific coordination domain - likely democratic mechanisms, epistemic defense, or resource allocation. This isn't just research infrastructure; it's a testing service that partners can use now. Researchers with proposals for new voting systems, deliberation protocols, or defense mechanisms can test them in our simulations against adversarial agents. As soon as simulation results look promising, we work with partners on small real-world pilots. The infrastructure development and policy testing happen in parallel, each informing the other.
details.howThisWorks: A researcher approaches us with a novel liquid democracy variant designed to resist manipulation. We implement it in our multi-agent environment, run adversarial red team attacks, measure outcomes, iterate on the design. If it performs well in simulation, we help pilot it with a local community or organization. Results feed back into improving both the mechanism and our simulation capabilities. This phase may reveal gaps in our foundational frameworks - if so, we revisit Phase 1. Success here means we have working infrastructure, proven methodology, early adopters, and a pipeline of policies to test.
